## Research Brief Overview
Researchers at the University of Florida, University of Texas at Dallas, and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute published a technical paper titled "BARE-AI: Bit-Flip Attack Resilience in AI Hardware through Built-in Performance Monitors."

## Abstract Excerpt
Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are integral to many safety critical systems, yet they remain highly vulnerable to bit-flip attacks (BFAs), where a few memory level perturbations can drastically degrade accuracy. Existing defenses incur significant hardware overhead, depend on retraining, or fail against targeted flips. We propose BARE-AI, a runtime framework that detects, localizes, and mitigates BFAs during AI inference.

## Citation & Source Link
Rahaman, Habibur, Swastik Bhattacharya, Sanjay Das, Kanad Basu, and Swarup Bhunia. "BARE-AI: Bit-Flip Attack Resilience in AI Hardware through Built-in Performance Monitors." arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.08739 (2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08739
documents.notes: Entry point coverage of UF/UTD/RPI built-in performance monitors for AI accelerators.
documents.title: On-Chip Monitors Detect Bit-Flip Attacks in AI Accelerators (UF, UT Dallas, RPI)

documents.content:
## Problem Statement: Bit-Flip Vulnerability in DNNs
Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are integral to many safety critical systems, yet they remain highly vulnerable to bit-flip attacks (BFAs), where a few memory level perturbations can drastically degrade accuracy. Existing defenses incur significant hardware overhead, depend on retraining, or fail against targeted flips.

## BARE-AI Architecture: APCs and PULSE
We propose BARE-AI, a runtime framework that detects, localizes, and mitigates BFAs during inference. BARE-AI introduces AI Performance Counters (APCs), lightweight hardware monitors in the accelerator datapath that capture per-layer activation statistics such as sparsity, entropy, kurtosis, and spectral shift. These are analyzed by the Predictive Unit for Layer Security Evaluation (PULSE), a compact detector trained offline as an ensemble of classifiers and realized on-chip as a small neural engine.

## Fault Localization and Weight Recovery
For explainability and recovery, BARE-AI introduces an Activation Shift Index (ASI) for layer level fault localization and a z-score based repair that resets anomalous weights toward clean layer statistics.

## Evaluation Across CNNs, ViTs, and LLMs
Across CNNs, Vision Transformers, and Large Language Models under random, targeted, adaptive, and magnitude based BFAs, BARE-AI achieves up to 98% detection accuracy on vision models and 74% to 95% on language models, restores near clean accuracy for CNNs and ViTs, and provides partial recovery for LLMs.

## Hardware Overhead at 28nm
Synthesized at 28nm, the monitoring infrastructure incurs under 3% energy, under 4% area, and about 10% latency overhead, with a configurable operating point that reduces latency overhead to about 6%. Unlike error correcting codes, whose redundancy grows with the number of tolerated flips, BARE-AI's overhead remains constant regardless of attack strength, making it attractive for resource constrained, safety critical edge applications such as autonomous systems, energy, and healthcare.
documents.notes: Core baseline for constant-overhead on-chip telemetry (APCs + PULSE) and ASI z-score weight recovery at 28nm.
documents.title: BARE-AI: Bit-Flip Attack Resilience in AI Hardware through Built-in Performance Monitors

documents.content:
## Fil-C Software Capabilities & Hardware Assumptions
Fil-C retrofits spatial and temporal memory safety onto C and C++ programs using software capabilities (InvisiCaps) checked on every pointer dereference. However, Fil-C relies on an unstated hardware assumption that DRAM reliably preserves capability metadata. In Fil-C, each heap pointer's upper-bound word is stored inline in ordinary DRAM without hardware integrity protection.

## Rowhammer Bit-Flip Attack Mechanism
A single 0-to-1 bit-flip induced by Rowhammer in a pointer's upper-bound metadata expands the pointer's permitted memory range by 2^k bytes. Because the runtime treats the corrupted upper bound as authoritative, it silently permits out-of-bounds reads and writes without raising any panic, signal, or exception.

## End-to-End Evaluation on DDR3 and DDR4 with TRR
Using both a deterministic fault-injection model and physical end-to-end Rowhammer reproduction on DDR3 and DDR4 memory equipped with Target Row Refresh (TRR), the authors demonstrate bounded read/write windows, secret disclosure, privilege escalation, and multi-tenant SQLite API key leakage, along with a probabilistic small-step operational semantics for memory fault reasoning.
documents.notes: Demonstrates how physical DRAM bit-flips subvert language-level software capabilities (InvisiCaps) even on DDR4 with TRR.
documents.title: A Rowhammer attack on Fil-C's software capabilities

documents.content:
## High-Bandwidth Memory & Chiplet Interconnect Threat Surface
Modern AI accelerators increasingly pair HBM3 and CXL memory subsystems with multi-die UCIe chiplet architectures. While error correcting codes (ECC) and Target Row Refresh (TRR) mitigate single-bit random faults, concentrated Rowhammer and targeted bit-flip attacks across shared memory channels threaten both Vision Transformers and Large Language Models.

## Co-Design of Memory Telemetry and Datapath Monitors
Combining inline memory controller telemetry with datapath AI Performance Counters (APCs) enables early anomaly detection before corrupted weights or pointer capability metadata propagate across UCIe die-to-die links.
documents.notes: Connects HBM/CXL memory subsystem defenses with on-chip datapath telemetry.
documents.title: Cross-Layer Resilience for HBM and UCIe Chiplet AI Accelerators Under Targeted Bit-Flip Faults

documents.content:
## Formal Verification of Runtime Security Monitors
Hardware performance monitors such as AI Performance Counters (APCs) and on-chip neural detectors like PULSE must themselves be verified against fault injection and timing side channels during RTL synthesis and place and route.

## Operational Semantics and Pre-Silicon Fault Simulation
By combining formal verification at the 28nm RTL boundary with probabilistic operational semantics for memory-level bit-flip perturbations, EDA toolflows can certify layer-level fault localization bounds prior to tapeout.
documents.notes: Bridges RTL formal verification and operational semantics for hardware fault monitors.
documents.title: Pre-Silicon Formal Verification of On-Chip Telemetry Monitors Against Fault Injection

documents.content:
## Unifying Hardware Datapath Telemetry and Software Capability Integrity
Both BARE-AI (arXiv:2610.08739v2) and the Fil-C Rowhammer study (arXiv:2610.33748) expose a critical cross-layer insight: neither Deep Neural Network weights nor language-level software capabilities (InvisiCaps) can assume uncorrupted DRAM when subjected to targeted bit-flip attacks.

## OntoLogic Knowledge Graph Synthesis
In our conceptual taxonomy, Bit-Flip Attacks bridge Hardware & Semiconductor Systems (AI Accelerators, Memory & Interconnects) and Security & Resilience (Memory Safety & Software Capabilities, Runtime Fault Localization & Recovery). Lightweight on-chip monitors (APCs, PULSE, ASI) and z-score statistical repair provide constant-overhead mitigation where traditional ECC or DDR4 Target Row Refresh (TRR) fall short.
documents.notes: Synthesis note linking AI accelerator weight resilience (BARE-AI) and C/C++ capability pointer integrity (Fil-C) for OntoLogic.
documents.title: Synthesis Note: Cross-Layer Bit-Flip Resilience Across AI Accelerators and Capability Runtimes

## Multi-Modal Formal Modeling Language for Hardware & Systems
UCLID5 is a formal modeling, verification, and synthesis framework and specification language designed for heterogeneous hardware and software systems. It enables compositional specification of Register-Transfer Level (RTL) datapaths, control logic, memory subsystems, and security monitors using first-order and temporal logic assertions.

## Bridging Chisel, FIRRTL, and SMT Solvers
In semiconductor design workflows, UCLID5 integrates with modern hardware construction languages such as Chisel and FIRRTL as well as SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA). Models are lowered to Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers and syntax-guided synthesis (SyGuS) engines for bounded model checking, inductive invariant synthesis, and hyperproperty verification.

## Verification of Secure Architectures and Accelerators
UCLID5 has been deployed to formally verify speculative execution mitigations, cryptographic accelerators, enclave isolation, and hardware fault-tolerance protocols prior to silicon tapeout.
documents.notes: Foundational formal modeling and verification language for hardware datapaths, Chisel/FIRRTL RTL, and security invariants.
documents.title: UCLID5: Multi-Modal Formal Modeling, Verification, and Synthesis

documents.content:
## Bottlenecks in Writing SystemVerilog Assertions (SVAs)
Formal Property Verification (FPV) in chip and semiconductor design relies heavily on SystemVerilog Assertions (SVAs) and Property Specification Language (PSL) to mathematically prove that Register-Transfer Level (RTL) implementations satisfy architectural specifications. Writing temporal logic assertions manually is error-prone and requires deep verification expertise.

## Unified Specification-and-RTL Knowledge Graph
AssertionForge constructs a unified hardware Knowledge Graph (KG) that fuses natural-language specification requirements with structural RTL signal interactions, finite-state machines, and clock/reset domains. Multi-resolution context retrieval over this graph prevents signal hallucination during automated SVA synthesis.

## Formal Property Verification Closure
Evaluated across industrial semiconductor IP blocks using commercial EDA formal verification engines, AssertionForge substantially increases syntax validity, temporal accuracy, and cone-of-influence coverage compared to baseline Large Language Model assertion generators.
documents.notes: Constructs a unified Knowledge Graph across natural-language specs and RTL to synthesize SystemVerilog Assertions (SVAs).
documents.title: AssertionForge: Enhancing Formal Verification Assertion Generation with Structured Representation of Specifications and RTL

documents.content:
## Solver-in-the-Loop Formal Assertion Synthesis
ProofLoop introduces a two-phase agentic framework that bridges natural-language hardware specifications, Register-Transfer Level (RTL) abstract syntax trees (ASTs), and formal verification languages such as SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA).

## Iterative Refinement with EDA Proof Engines
In Phase A, ProofLoop queries an AST-indexed structural representation of the Verilog/SystemVerilog design to ground clock, reset, and handshake signals. In Phase B, a solver-in-the-loop agent invokes commercial formal verification engines such as Cadence JasperGold, parses counterexample traces and vacuity reports, and iteratively repairs candidate SVA properties until mathematical proof closure is achieved.

## Implications for Semiconductor Verification Flows
Coupling deterministic formal solvers with automated assertion synthesis eliminates vacuous properties and accelerates pre-silicon verification of complex SoC interconnects and AI accelerator datapaths.
documents.notes: Solver-in-the-loop ReAct agent coupling AST-indexed RTL analysis with JasperGold formal proof feedback to refine SVA assertions.
documents.title: ProofLoop: From Language to Logic — Bridging LLMs and Formal Representations for RTL Assertion Generation

documents.content:
## Behavioral Equivalence in Hardware Verification Languages
Evaluating automated SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) generators requires distinguishing true behavioral temporal properties from brittle assertions tied to incidental RTL coding style. EquivSVA provides a formally verified benchmark organized around behavior families of structurally distinct RTL implementations sharing identical interface specifications.

## Formal Equivalence & Metamorphic Verification
Every gold SVA assertion in EquivSVA is mechanically verified using formal property verification (FPV) and SMT-based equivalence checking across pipelined, FSM-encoded, and Chisel/FIRRTL-generated RTL variants.

## Advancing Robust Semiconductor Verification
EquivSVA enables rigorous benchmarking of formal verification language translators, theorem-proving hardware frameworks (Kami, Coq), and LLM-assisted assertion synthesis pipelines.
documents.notes: Formally verified dataset of behavioral SVA assertions across structurally distinct but functionally equivalent RTL designs.
documents.title: EquivSVA: A Formally Verified Dataset of Behavioral Assertions Across Equivalent RTL Implementations

documents.content:
## Research Scope & Core Languages: Formal verification languages in chip and semiconductor design
In chip and semiconductor design, Formal Verification Languages provide the mathematical foundation for specifying and proving Register-Transfer Level (RTL) and architectural invariants before silicon fabrication. The industrial backbone comprises IEEE 1800 SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and IEEE 1850 Property Specification Language (PSL) for linear temporal logic (LTL) Formal Property Verification (FPV), complemented by multi-modal verification and hardware construction languages including UCLID5 (SMT-backed datapath/control modeling), Chisel/FIRRTL (ChiselFV), and Coq-embedded theorem-proving frameworks such as Kami.

## Knowledge-Graph & Solver-in-the-Loop Assertion Synthesis
Recent research synthesized in this collection — UCLID5: Multi-Modal Formal Modeling, Verification, and Synthesis (arxiv-2208.03699); AssertionForge: Enhancing Formal Verification Assertion Generation with Structured Representation of Specifications and RTL (arxiv-2503.19174); ProofLoop: From Language to Logic — Bridging LLMs and Formal Representations for RTL Assertion Generation (arxiv-2604.23100); EquivSVA: A Formally Verified Dataset of Behavioral Assertions Across Equivalent RTL Implementations (arxiv-2609.26751) — addresses the manual bottleneck of authoring temporal logic assertions. Frameworks like AssertionForge construct unified Knowledge Graphs fusing natural-language specs and RTL structure, while agentic solver-in-the-loop systems like ProofLoop interact directly with commercial EDA formal engines (Cadence JasperGold and SMT solvers) to iteratively refine SVA assertions until formal proof closure.

## Cross-Layer Integration with Hardware Telemetry & Security
Within our OntoLogic-ready knowledge graph, formal verification languages connect pre-silicon EDA verification with runtime hardware security monitors (such as BARE-AI's 28nm AI Performance Counters and PULSE neural detectors) and probabilistic operational semantics for memory-level bit-flip resilience (such as Rowhammer analysis on Fil-C software capabilities).

## Graph Analysis & Monotonic Theories in SMT
Encoding complex graph-theoretic properties — such as reachability, shortest paths, maximum s-t flow, minimum spanning trees, and directed acyclic graph (DAG) acyclicity — directly into Boolean SAT or standard SMT bit-vector/integer theories causes severe formula blowup and poor solver propagation. MonoSAT introduces a general DPLL(T) framework for finite monotonic theories that integrates dedicated incremental graph algorithms directly inside an SMT solver.

## Under- and Over-Approximation Theory Propagation
MonoSAT maintains dual under-approximating and over-approximating graphs as Boolean edge variables are assigned during Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) search. When a graph predicate (such as reachability or cycle-freeness) becomes violated, MonoSAT extracts a succinct conflict clause (cut-set or witness path) in polynomial time, orders of magnitude faster than propositional encodings.

## Applications in Network Verification, Routing & Ontology Graphs
MonoSAT powers formal cloud network reachability analysis, circuit routing, dependency graph resolution in software package managers, and structural acyclicity/subsumption checks in large-scale knowledge graphs and ontologies.
documents.notes: Pioneering SMT framework (DPLL(T)) for finite monotonic theories supporting native graph predicates (reachability, shortest path, max-flow, acyclicity).
documents.title: MonoSAT: Modulo Theories for Graphs, Networks, and Geometry

documents.content:
## Next-Generation DPLL(T) SMT Architecture
cvc5 is an industrial-strength Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) and Syntax-Guided Synthesis (SyGuS) solver built on a modular CDCL(T) / DPLL(T) core. It combines high-performance Boolean SAT solving with decision procedures for bit-vectors, arrays, floating-point arithmetic, strings and regular expressions, algebraic datatypes, and quantifier instantiation.

## Finite Sets, Relations & Ontology Constraint Solving
Uniquely suited to graph analysis and formal ontologies, cvc5 provides native decision procedures for the Theory of Finite Sets and the Theory of Finite Relations (including transitive closure, relational join, and cardinality constraints). These relational theories enable direct SMT encoding of OWL Description Logic axioms, Alloy structural models, and SHACL knowledge-graph validation rules.

## Software Development & Deductive Verification
In software engineering, cvc5 serves as the automated reasoning backend for deductive verifiers (Dafny, Spark/Ada, Viper), smart-contract auditors, cloud IAM policy analyzers (AWS Zelkova), and symbolic execution engines.
documents.notes: Industrial-strength DPLL(T) SMT and SyGuS solver supporting strings, finite sets, relations, bit-vectors, and algebraic datatypes.
documents.title: cvc5: A Versatile and Industrial-Strength SMT Solver

documents.content:
## Path-Constraint Solving with SAT and SMT Solvers
Symbolic execution transforms software development, automated test generation, and vulnerability discovery by executing programs over symbolic inputs rather than concrete values. At every conditional branch, the symbolic execution engine (such as KLEE, SAGE, or CBMC) queries an SMT solver (Z3, STP, or cvc5) over the Theory of Bit-Vectors and Arrays (QF_ABV) to decide path feasibility and synthesize concrete bug-triggering inputs.

## Constraint Caching, Slicing & Heap Graph Modeling
Because SMT solver queries dominate symbolic execution runtime, modern software analysis tools employ counterexample-guided constraint caching, independent clause slicing, and array-theory memory modeling to reason about pointer aliasing and heap data structures (linked lists, trees, and control-flow graphs).

## Memory Safety & Security Vulnerability Detection
Coupling SAT/SMT solvers with symbolic execution and bounded model checking uncovers spatial/temporal memory safety violations, integer overflows, and invariant breaches across systems software.
documents.notes: Comprehensive study of SAT/SMT constraint solving in symbolic execution (KLEE, SAGE, Angr) for automated test generation and vulnerability discovery.
documents.title: A Survey of Symbolic Execution Techniques for Software Development and Verification

documents.content:
## Encoding OWL Ontologies & Description Logics into SAT/SMT
Formal ontologies (OWL 2, SKOS, and Description Logics such as EL, ALC, and SHQ) define hierarchical concept taxonomies (TBox) and relational knowledge graph assertions (ABox). By encoding concept subsumption, disjointness, and role inclusion axioms into Horn-SAT and Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) SAT formulas, automated reasoners classify ratusan-thousand-concept ontologies in seconds.

## Concrete Domains & Numerical Constraints via SMT
Real-world engineering and scientific ontologies require reasoning simultaneously over taxonomic hierarchies and concrete numerical domains (thresholds, intervals, unit conversions, and cardinality bounds). Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) bridges this gap by combining Boolean ontology axiom propagation with Linear Real/Integer Arithmetic (LRA/LIA) and Uninterpreted Functions (EUF).

## OntoLogic Integration & Knowledge Graph Verification
SAT/SMT-backed ontology reasoning detects unsatisfiable classes, cyclic taxonomy regressions, and SHACL constraint violations across evolving semantic knowledge graphs.
documents.notes: Demonstrates how encoding Description Logic (EL+/ALC) TBox/ABox ontologies into CDCL SAT and SMT enables ultra-fast classification, subsumption, and datatype constraint checking.
documents.title: SAT and SMT-Based Automated Reasoning for Description Logics and Formal Ontologies

documents.content:
## SAT & SMT Decision Procedures Across Software, Graphs, and Ontologies: SAT and SMT solvers applications in software development, graph analysis, and ontologies
Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) SAT solvers and DPLL(T) Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers (such as Z3 and cvc5) serve as the computational backbone for modern automated reasoning. By combining Boolean constraint propagation with specialized background theories — bit-vectors, arrays, strings, linear arithmetic, finite sets, and relations — SMT solvers unify software verification, combinatorial graph analysis, and formal ontology reasoning.

## Symbolic Execution, Monotonic Graph Theories & Description Logics
Primary literature synthesized in this collection — MonoSAT: Modulo Theories for Graphs, Networks, and Geometry (arxiv-1402.4677); cvc5: A Versatile and Industrial-Strength SMT Solver (arxiv-2201.04663); A Survey of Symbolic Execution Techniques for Software Development and Verification (arxiv-1610.00502); SAT and SMT-Based Automated Reasoning for Description Logics and Formal Ontologies (arxiv-1507.01763) — spans three synergistic pillars: (1) **Software Development & Symbolic Execution** (KLEE, CBMC, Dafny, cvc5), where path constraints over bit-vectors and arrays synthesize bug-triggering inputs and prove memory-safety invariants; (2) **Graph Analysis Modulo Theories** (MonoSAT), where monotonic graph predicates (reachability, shortest path, maximum s-t flow, minimum spanning tree, and DAG acyclicity) are decided natively inside DPLL(T) without propositional blowup; and (3) **Ontology & Description Logic Reasoning** (OWL 2, EL/ALC, SHACL, OntoLogic), where TBox/ABox concept subsumption, consistency, and numerical datatype constraints reduce directly to Horn-SAT and SMT.

## Cross-Domain Integration in the Reading-DB Knowledge Graph
Within our OntoLogic-ready knowledge base, SAT and SMT solvers bridge software capability verification (Fil-C memory safety), hardware formal verification languages (UCLID5, SVA, ProofLoop), and taxonomic ontology validation.

## Problem Statement & Context
Translating complex natural language specifications into formal First-Order Logic (FOL) for automated theorem provers and SMT solvers (such as cvc5 and Z3) frequently suffers from syntactic hallucinations and semantic drift when performed via direct end-to-end Large Language Model generation.

## Proposed Mechanism: AST-Guided & Grammar-Constrained Translation
NL2LOGIC inserts an explicit Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) intermediate representation between a recursive LLM semantic parser and a deterministic, grammar-constrained FOL code generator. By decomposing natural language statements into typed logical subtrees before emitting solver-ready First-Order Logic formulas, inference can be reliably delegated to SAT/SMT decision procedures and ontology reasoners.

## Evaluation & Why It Matters (via kitsumiko/papers)
NL2LOGIC reaches 99% syntactic accuracy and up to 30% higher semantic correctness than prior LLM logic-parsing methods on FOLIO, LogicNLI, and ProofWriter, lifting downstream formal reasoning accuracy by 31% when integrated into Logic-LM. Curated from kitsumiko/papers (Reasoning & Agents).
documents.notes: Curated from kitsumiko/papers (learning/reasoning.md). Bridges LLM semantic parsing with solver-ready First-Order Logic for OntoLogic and cvc5.
documents.title: NL2LOGIC: AST-Guided Translation of Natural Language into First-Order Logic with Large Language Models

## Problem Statement & Context
Standard autoregressive transformers and frontier Large Language Models lack sound deductive guarantees and routinely fail on combinatorial constraint satisfaction problems requiring deep, contradiction-free propagation.

## Proposed Mechanism: Abstract Lattice Projection & Sound Deduction
Lattice Deduction Transformers introduce a recurrent transformer architecture that projects its latent state onto an abstract lattice between forward passes so that each pass acts as a formally sound deduction step. The model is trained on-policy inside a constraint-solver-style loop with abstract-interpretation-based supervision.

## Evaluation & Why It Matters (via kitsumiko/papers)
An 800K-parameter Lattice Deduction Transformer reaches 100% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme and Snowflake Sudoku, and a 1.8M-parameter variant achieves 99.9% on Maze-Hard, whereas frontier LLMs score 0% on all three benchmarks—demonstrating that abstract interpretation gives compact recurrent reasoners both formal correctness and deductive competence. Curated from kitsumiko/papers (Novel Architectures & Theory).
documents.notes: Curated from kitsumiko/papers (learning/architectures.md). Connects abstract interpretation and lattice domain theory with recurrent neural deduction.
documents.title: Lattice Deduction Transformers

## Problem Statement & Context
Empirical red-teaming and discrete prompt fuzzing cannot provide formal completeness or soundness guarantees for LLM safety guardrail classifiers deployed in security-critical pipelines.

## Proposed Mechanism: Convex Pre-Activation Certification via SVD Hyper-Rectangles
Beyond Red-Teaming shifts guardrail formal verification from the discrete token input space to the classifier pre-activation layer, where harmful prompt embeddings form convex regions certifiable via the monotonicity of the sigmoid classification head. It constructs exact SVD-aligned hyper-rectangles and probabilistic Gaussian Mixture Models to certify safe and unsafe regions.

## Evaluation & Why It Matters (via kitsumiko/papers)
Formal region certification exposes large safety coverage gaps in BERT-based guardrails (55-90% certified coverage) compared to more stable GPT-2 and Llama guardrail classifiers (~80-90% coverage). Curated from kitsumiko/papers (Security, Safety & Robustness).

documents.title: Beyond Red-Teaming: Formal Guarantees of LLM Guardrail Classifiers

## Problem Statement & Context
Large-scale combinatorial optimization and graph-structured constraint problems often bottleneck CPU-bound Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) and SMT solvers when scaling to massive instance sizes.

## Proposed Mechanism: Hardware-Aware CUDA Block Evolution
cuGenOpt introduces a GPU-accelerated general-purpose metaheuristic framework built on a "one CUDA block evolves one solution" architecture with hardware-aware shared memory and register resource management across GPU generations (T4, V100, A800).

## Evaluation & Why It Matters (via kitsumiko/papers)
Outperforms general MIP solvers by orders of magnitude on large-scale combinatorial optimization benchmarks while maintaining portability across GPU accelerator generations. Curated from kitsumiko/papers (Hardware & Systems).

## Problem Statement & Context
Evaluating autonomous LLM agents on software security engineering requires authentic, reproducible vulnerability environments rather than synthetic static code snippets.

## Proposed Mechanism: Multi-Agent Verified Vulnerability Scaffold
SEC-bench introduces the first fully automated benchmarking framework for evaluating LLM agents on real-world software security tasks, using a multi-agent scaffold to construct verified vulnerability datasets complete with reproducible Proof-of-Concept (PoC) exploits and validated patches.

## Evaluation & Why It Matters (via kitsumiko/papers)
Reveals significant capability gaps in frontier coding agents (18% PoC exploit generation, 34% automated vulnerability patching), establishing a rigorous baseline for software verification and security agents. Curated from kitsumiko/papers (Security, Safety & Robustness).

## Problem Statement & Context
Reasoning models increasingly trade off discrete token emission (Chain-of-Thought) against continuous hidden-state iteration (Latent Thought), yet lacked a formal complexity-theoretic comparison.

## Proposed Mechanism: Complexity & Expressivity Separation
Establishes a formal theoretical separation proving that latent thought enables exponentially more efficient parallel circuit computation than inherently sequential Chain-of-Thought, whereas discrete CoT uniquely supports approximate counting and calibrated stochastic sampling.

## Evaluation & Why It Matters (via kitsumiko/papers)
Provides principled mathematical criteria for choosing between discrete-token deduction and continuous latent recurrence (such as Lattice Deduction Transformers) based on task recursion depth and stochasticity requirements. Curated from kitsumiko/papers (Reasoning & Agents).

## Executive Synthesis & Attribution
This synthesis note bridges seven high-signal research papers curated from the [`kitsumiko/papers`](https://github.com/kitsumiko/papers) AI/ML Research Curriculum into our hardware security, RTL formal verification, and SAT/SMT OntoLogic knowledge graph. The full 320-paper curriculum sits alongside this database in [`bsommers/ai-curriculum-db`](https://github.com/bsommers/ai-curriculum-db).

## Neuro-Symbolic Deduction & Solver-Ready Logic
NL2LOGIC (`arxiv-2602.13237`) and Lattice Deduction Transformers (`arxiv-2605.08605`), together with the formal separation of Chain-of-Thought and Latent Thought (`arxiv-2509.25239`), connect neural architectures directly to First-Order Logic (FOL), abstract interpretation lattices, and DPLL(T) SMT solvers (`cvc5`, `arxiv-2201.04663`).

## Formal Safety Certification & Hardware-Rooted Verification
Beyond Red-Teaming (`arxiv-2605.10901`) brings formal region certification to neural guardrail classifiers, SEC-bench (`openreview-sec-bench-2025`) benchmarks autonomous security agents on verified vulnerabilities, cuGenOpt (`arxiv-2603.19163`) accelerates combinatorial optimization on GPUs, and How to Catch a GPU (`arxiv-2607.22619`) links on-chip accelerator telemetry (`BARE-AI`, `arxiv-2610.08739v2`) to international hardware verification agreements.

## Problem Statement & Context
Large Language Models (LLMs) have risen significantly in popularity and are increasingly being adopted across multiple applications. These LLMs are heavily aligned to resist engaging in illegal or unethical topics as a means to avoid contributing to responsible AI harms. However, a recent line of attacks, known as jailbreaks, seek to overcome this alignment. Intuitively, jailbreak attacks aim to narrow the gap between what the model can do and what it is willing to do.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
In this paper, we introduce a novel jailbreak attack called Crescendo. Unlike existing jailbreak methods, Crescendo is a simple multi-turn jailbreak that interacts with the model in a seemingly benign manner. It begins with a general prompt or question about the task at hand and then gradually escalates the dialogue by referencing the model's replies progressively leading to a successful jailbreak. We evaluate Crescendo on various public systems, including ChatGPT, Gemini Pro, Gemini-Ultra, LlaMA-2 70b and LlaMA-3 70b Chat, and Anthropic Chat.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
Our results demonstrate the strong efficacy of Crescendo, with it achieving high attack success rates across all evaluated models and tasks. Furthermore, we present Crescendomation, a tool that automates the Crescendo attack and demonstrate its efficacy against state-of-the-art models through our evaluations. Crescendomation surpasses other state-of-the-art jailbreaking techniques on the AdvBench subset dataset, achieving 29-61% higher performance on GPT-4 and 49-71% on Gemini-Pro. Finally, we also demonstrate Crescendo's ability to jailbreak multimodal models.
documents.notes: Primary attack paper: the benign-looking, gradually escalating multi-turn jailbreak (Crescendo) and its automated variant Crescendomation. Defenses in this pack are largely motivated by it. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: Great, Now Write an Article About That: The Crescendo Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreak Attack

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, but their deployment has exposed critical vulnerabilities, particularly to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety alignments. Guardrails--external defense mechanisms that monitor and control LLM interactions--have emerged as a promising solution.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
However, the current landscape of LLM guardrails is fragmented, lacking a unified taxonomy and comprehensive evaluation framework. In this Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) paper, we present the first holistic analysis of jailbreak guardrails for LLMs.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
We propose a novel, multi-dimensional taxonomy that categorizes guardrails along six key dimensions, and introduce a Security-Efficiency-Utility evaluation framework to assess their practical effectiveness. Through extensive analysis and experiments, we identify the strengths and limitations of existing guardrail approaches, provide insights into optimizing their defense mechanisms, and explore their universality across attack types. Our work offers a structured foundation for future research and development, aiming to guide the principled advancement and deployment of robust LLM guardrails. The code is available at https://github.com/xunguangwang/SoK4JailbreakGuardrails.
documents.notes: SoK on jailbreak guardrails: six-dimension taxonomy and a Security-Efficiency-Utility evaluation framework. Background reference for comparing guardrail approaches. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: SoK: Evaluating Jailbreak Guardrails for Large Language Models

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly operate across domains such as robotics, virtual assistants, and web automation. However, their stochastic decision-making introduces safety risks that are difficult to anticipate during execution. Existing runtime monitoring frameworks, such as AgentSpec, primarily rely on reactive safety rules that detect violations only when unsafe behavior is imminent or has already occurred, limiting their ability to handle long-horizon dependencies.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
We present ProbGuard, a proactive runtime monitoring framework for LLM agents that anticipates safety violations through probabilistic risk prediction. ProbGuard abstracts agent executions into symbolic states and learns a Discrete-Time Markov Chain (DTMC) from execution traces to model behavioral dynamics. At runtime, the monitor estimates the probability that execution will remain safe from the current state, and triggers an intervention when this probability falls below a user-defined threshold.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
To improve robustness, ProbGuard incorporates semantic validity constraints in the abstraction and admits a PAC-style analysis that characterizes the sample complexity required to certify the learned model under standard assumptions. We evaluate ProbGuard in two safety-critical domains: autonomous driving and embodied household agents. Across evaluated scenarios, ProbGuard consistently predicts traffic law violations and collisions in advance, with warnings up to 15.84 seconds at a threshold yielding no false alarms, and up to 38.66 seconds at stricter thresholds. In embodied agent tasks, ProbGuard's re-prompting intervention mode reduces unsafe behavior by 65.37% relative to the unmonitored baseline while retaining 80.4% of the baseline task completion; a stricter halting configuration reduces unsafe behavior by 93.60% at a larger cost in completion.
documents.notes: Evaluated on autonomous driving and embodied household agents, not on chat or security-conversation traces. Relevant here as a trajectory-prediction technique (DTMC over abstracted execution states). Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: ProbGuard: Proactive Runtime Monitoring for LLM Agent Safety via Probabilistic Prediction

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Guardrail models are essential for ensuring the safety of Large Language Model (LLM) deployments, but processing full multi-turn conversation histories incurs significant computational cost. We propose Defensive M2S, a training paradigm that fine-tunes guardrail models on Multi-turn to Single-turn (M2S) compressed conversations rather than complete dialogue histories. We provide a formal complexity analysis showing that M2S reduces training cost from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ for $n$-turn conversations.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
Empirically, on our training dataset (779 samples, avg. 10.6 turns), M2S requires only 169K tokens compared to 15.7M tokens for the multi-turn baseline -- a 93$\times$ reduction. We evaluate Defensive M2S across three guardrail model families (LlamaGuard, Nemotron, Qwen3Guard) and three compression templates (hyphenize, numberize, pythonize) on SafeDialBench, a comprehensive multi-turn jailbreak benchmark.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
Our best configuration, Qwen3Guard with hyphenize compression, achieves 93.8% attack detection recall while reducing inference tokens by 94.6% (from 3,231 to 173 tokens per conversation). This represents a 38.9 percentage point improvement over the baseline while dramatically reducing both training and inference costs. Our findings demonstrate that M2S compression can serve as an effective efficiency technique for guardrail deployment, enabling scalable safety screening of long multi-turn conversations.
documents.notes: Compresses multi-turn history to single-turn for guardrail training and inference (efficiency angle). Single-author; results on SafeDialBench. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: Defensive M2S: Training Guardrail Models on Compressed Multi-turn Conversations

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
The proliferation of agentic AI coding assistants, including Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and emerging skill-based architectures, has fundamentally transformed software development workflows. These systems leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) integrated with external tools, file systems, and shell access through protocols like the Model Context Protocol (MCP). However, this expanded capability surface introduces critical security vulnerabilities.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
In this \textbf{Systematization of Knowledge (SoK)} paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of prompt injection attacks targeting agentic coding assistants. We propose a novel three-dimensional taxonomy categorizing attacks across \textit{delivery vectors}, \textit{attack modalities}, and \textit{propagation behaviors}. Our meta-analysis synthesizes findings from 78 recent studies (2021--2026), consolidating evidence that attack success rates against state-of-the-art defenses exceed 85\% when adaptive attack strategies are employed.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
We systematically catalog 42 distinct attack techniques spanning input manipulation, tool poisoning, protocol exploitation, multimodal injection, and cross-origin context poisoning. Through critical analysis of 18 defense mechanisms reported in prior work, we identify that most achieve less than 50\% mitigation against sophisticated adaptive attacks. We contribute: (1) a unified taxonomy bridging disparate attack classifications, (2) the first systematic analysis of skill-based architecture vulnerabilities with concrete exploit chains, and (3) a defense-in-depth framework grounded in the limitations we identify. Our findings indicate that the security community must treat prompt injection as a first-class vulnerability class requiring architectural-level mitigations rather than ad-hoc filtering approaches.
documents.notes: SoK meta-analysis (78 studies, 42 attack techniques, 18 defenses). Figures are the authors' consolidation of prior work, not new measurements. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic Coding Assistants: A Systematic Analysis of Vulnerabilities in Skills, Tools, and Protocol Ecosystems

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Multi-turn prompt injection attacks distribute malicious intent across multiple conversation turns, exploiting the assumption that each turn is evaluated independently. While single-turn detection has been extensively studied, no published formula exists for aggregating per-turn pattern scores into a conversation-level risk score at the proxy layer -- without invoking an LLM.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
We identify a fundamental flaw in the intuitive weighted-average approach: it converges to the per-turn score regardless of turn count, meaning a 20-turn persistent attack scores identically to a single suspicious turn. Drawing on analogies from change-point detection (CUSUM), Bayesian belief updating, and security risk-based alerting, we propose peak + accumulation scoring -- a formula combining peak single-turn risk, persistence ratio, and category diversity.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
Evaluated on 10,654 multi-turn conversations -- 588 attacks sourced from WildJailbreak adversarial prompts and 10,066 benign conversations from WildChat -- the formula achieves 90.8% recall at 1.20% false positive rate with an F1 of 85.9%. A sensitivity analysis over the persistence parameter reveals a phase transition at rho ~ 0.4, where recall jumps 12 percentage points with negligible FPR increase. We release the scoring algorithm, pattern library, and evaluation harness as open source.
documents.notes: Single-author. Practical, LLM-free conversation-level scoring formula for a proxy; shows why a weighted average fails to catch persistent attacks. Dataset: WildJailbreak attacks vs WildChat benign. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: Peak + Accumulation: A Proxy-Level Scoring Formula for Multi-Turn LLM Attack Detection

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
While Large Language Model (LLM) capabilities have scaled, safety guardrails remain largely stateless, treating multi-turn dialogues as a series of disconnected events. This lack of temporal awareness facilitates a "Safety Gap" where adversarial tactics, like Crescendo and ActorAttack, slowly bleed malicious intent across turn boundaries to bypass stateless filters.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
We introduce DeepContext, a stateful monitoring framework designed to map the temporal trajectory of user intent. DeepContext discards the isolated evaluation model in favor of a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) architecture that ingests a sequence of fine-tuned turn-level embeddings.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
By propagating a hidden state across the conversation, DeepContext captures the incremental accumulation of risk that stateless models overlook. Our evaluation demonstrates that DeepContext significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-turn jailbreak detection, achieving a state-of-the-art F1 score of 0.84, which represents a substantial improvement over both hyperscaler cloud-provider guardrails and leading open-weight models such as Llama-Prompt-Guard-2 (0.67) and Granite-Guardian (0.67). Furthermore, DeepContext maintains a sub-20ms inference overhead on a T4 GPU, ensuring viability for real-time applications. These results suggest that modeling the sequential evolution of intent is a more effective and computationally efficient alternative to deploying massive, stateless models.
documents.notes: Stateful (RNN over turn embeddings) detector for Crescendo/ActorAttack-style intent drift; reports F1 0.84 vs 0.67 for Llama-Prompt-Guard-2 and Granite-Guardian with sub-20ms overhead on a T4. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: DeepContext: Stateful Real-Time Detection of Multi-Turn Adversarial Intent Drift in LLMs

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Agentic AI systems introduce a security surface that is qualitatively different from that of stateless LLMs. They persist memory, invoke external tools, coordinate with peer agents, and operate across sessions, allowing attacks to emerge not only at the prompt interface but also through architectural state, delegated authority, and long-horizon interactions. Existing security taxonomies, however, primarily organize threats by attack type, such as prompt injection or jailbreaking, and therefore obscure where in the agentic stack a threat arises and over what timescale it manifests.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
We propose the Layered Attack Surface Model (\lasm), a structural taxonomy for agentic AI security. \lasm decomposes the agentic stack into seven layers -- Foundation, Cognitive, Memory, Tool Execution, Multi-Agent Coordination, Ecosystem, and Governance -- and augments them with a four-class temporality axis covering instantaneous, session-persistent, cross-session cumulative, and sub-session-stack threats. We use this 7$\times$4 framework to analyze 116 papers from 2021--2026.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
The resulting map reveals that the upper layers of the agentic stack remain sharply under-explored, especially for long-horizon and stack-propagating threats; multiple documented attack regions have no corresponding defenses; and current benchmarks provide no coverage for cross-session or sub-session-stack failure modes. We further derive a cross-layer defense taxonomy, defense recipes for canonical attack classes, and a dependency DAG that separates near-term engineering gaps from fundamental research challenges. We release the per-paper coding, robustness scripts, and a reference Agent Bill of Materials schema to support reproducible analysis.
documents.notes: Layered Attack Surface Model: 7 layers x 4 temporalities (instantaneous, session-persistent, cross-session cumulative, sub-session-stack) over 116 papers. Reports that benchmarks give no coverage of cross-session or sub-session-stack failures. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: A Systematic Survey of Security Threats and Defenses in LLM-Based AI Agents: A Layered Attack Surface Framework

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Large Language Model (LLM)-powered agents demonstrate strong capabilities in autonomous task execution, tool use, and multi-step reasoning. However, their increasing autonomy also introduces a new attack surface: adversarial interactions can manipulate agent behavior through direct prompt injection, indirect content attacks, and multi-turn escalation strategies. Existing defense strategies focus on prompt-level filtering and rule-based guardrails, which are often insufficient when risk emerges gradually across interaction sequences.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
In this work, we propose a complementary defense mechanism: a low-latency fraud detection layer for detecting adversarial interaction patterns in LLM-powered agents. Instead of determining whether a single prompt is malicious, our approach models risk over interaction trajectories using structured runtime features derived from prompt characteristics, session dynamics, tool usage, execution context, and fraud-inspired signals. The detection layer can be implemented using lightweight models leading to low-latency real-time deployments.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
To evaluate the framework, we construct a synthetic corpus of 12,000 multi-turn agent interactions generated from parameterized templates that simulate realistic agentic workflows. Using 42 structured features and an XGBoost classifier, our detector achieves over 9 times faster than LLM-based detectors. Through the experiment and ablation studies, our work suggests that interaction-level behavioral detection should become a core component of deployment-time defense for LLM-powered agents.
documents.notes: Evaluated on a synthetic corpus of 12,000 template-generated interactions, not organic traces. The arXiv listing shows a newer-version title 'A Fraud-Detection-Inspired Framework for LLM Agents Security'; title here is from the abstract page as fetched. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: A Low-Latency Fraud Detection Layer for Detecting Adversarial Interaction Patterns in LLM-Powered Agents

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Modern AI agents execute real-world side effects through tool calls such as file operations, shell commands, HTTP requests, and database queries. A single unsafe action, including accidental deletion, credential exposure, or data exfiltration, can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses are incomplete: post-hoc benchmarks measure behavior after execution, static guardrails miss obfuscation and multi-step context, and infrastructure sandboxes constrain where code runs without understanding what an action means.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
We present AgentTrust, a runtime safety layer that intercepts agent tool calls before execution and returns a structured verdict: allow, warn, block, or review. AgentTrust combines a shell deobfuscation normalizer, SafeFix suggestions for safer alternatives, RiskChain detection for multi-step attack chains, and a cache-aware LLM-as-Judge for ambiguous inputs. We release a 300-scenario benchmark across six risk categories and an additional 630 independently constructed real-world adversarial scenarios.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
On the internal benchmark, the production-only ruleset achieves 95.0% verdict accuracy and 73.7% risk-level accuracy at low-millisecond end-to-end latency. On the 630-scenario benchmark, evaluated under a patched ruleset and not claimed as zero-shot, AgentTrust achieves 96.7% verdict accuracy, including about 93% on shell-obfuscated payloads. AgentTrust is released under the AGPL-3.0 license and provides a Model Context Protocol server for MCP-compatible agents.
documents.notes: Single-author, AGPL-3.0, ships an MCP server. Its RiskChain module targets multi-step attack chains. The 630-scenario result is stated by the author to be under a patched ruleset and not zero-shot. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: AgentTrust: Runtime Safety Evaluation and Interception for AI Agent Tool Use

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks pose a growing threat to LLMs by exploiting conversational dynamics such as gradual escalation and cross-turn coordination. Existing defenses either rely on costly retraining -- often degrading model utility -- or apply single-turn analysis independently at each turn, failing to capture how risk accumulates along interaction trajectories.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
We observe that safety behavior in multi-turn interaction is trajectory-dependent: dialogue history continuously reshapes the model's conditioning context, making it insufficient to evaluate each turn in isolation. Motivated by this insight, we present THRD, the first training-free framework that explicitly models temporal risk accumulation for multi-turn jailbreak defense.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
THRD integrates four modules: a Turn-level Risk Assessor (TRA) for instantaneous risk estimation, a Historical Context Analyzer (HCA) for cross-turn intent escalation detection, a Response Evaluator (RE) for identifying facilitative outputs, and a Decision Module that combines these signals through a time-evolving scoring mechanism with attenuation-based modulation and trend-aware adjustment. Experiments against state-of-the-art multi-turn attacks -- including tree-search-based and multi-agent collaborative methods -- across two target models show that THRD reduces ASR to 0.2--4.0% while preserving model utility within 1.5% degradation on MMLU and GSM8K. Ablation studies confirm non-redundant module contributions and stable cross-architecture generalization. Analysis of first rejection triggers reveals that over 70% of multi-turn attacks require Turn~2 or later to detect, validating the necessity of explicit temporal aggregation.
documents.notes: Training-free defense with four modules (turn risk, historical context, response evaluator, decision). Reports ASR 0.2-4.0% and that over 70% of multi-turn attacks need Turn 2 or later to detect. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: THRD: A Training-Free Multi-Turn Defense Framework for Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks on large language models (LLMs) reveal a mismatch in current guardrails: they operate on individual turns, while attacks unfold as trajectories across conversations. We propose a shift from content to dynamics, modeling conversations as paths in representation space and asking whether adversarial intent is encoded early in their geometry.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
We introduce PsychoPass, a framework that extracts geometric features from conversation trajectories in embedding space to predict a potential attack before harmful content is produced. These features achieve near-perfect performance in na\"ive classifiers, which is largely explained by the inclusion of number of turns as a feature.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
After removing this confound, a smaller but consistent geometric signal remains, with classification performance that does not depend meaningfully on encoder choice. Crucially, this signal appears early in the conversation: attack outcomes remain above chance from short prefixes alone, more reliably than baseline guardrails. A supporting theoretical analysis explains these findings via a decomposition of length and shape, a detection bound based on prefix length, and encoder invariance. Together, these results show that adversarial conversations leave an early, representation-robust geometric fingerprint suitable for online monitoring.
documents.notes: Caveat from the abstract itself: near-perfect classifier scores are largely explained by number of turns as a confound; after removing it a smaller but consistent geometric signal remains. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: PsychoPass: Geometric Profiling of Multi-Turn Adversarial LLM Conversations

documents.content:
## Problem Statement & Context
Tool-using LLM agents increasingly execute high-impact actions, making runtime safety monitoring essential. We present NEXUS (Neural EXecution Utility and Safety), a structured-plan safety monitor that applies a formal intervention policy to select among four actions: allow, block, request confirmation, or request revision. NEXUS combines deterministic safety rules, argument-level inspection, and a calibrated logistic-regression risk score for graded escalation.

## Proposed Mechanism & Architecture
On a 128-instance synthetic benchmark, NEXUS achieves an F1 score of 0.949 and a 4-class intervention accuracy of 0.6406, outperforming rule-only intervention selection by 27.3 percentage points. It also improves over rule-only on R-Judge (F1 = 0.861 vs. 0.849), matches rule-only on AgentHarm due to threat-model limits, and achieves 0% ASR at 99% control allow on IPI.

## Evaluation & Key Findings
On the rule-blind NEXUS-Stress benchmark, NEXUS reaches an F1 score of 0.881, highlighting the difficulty of fine-grained intervention routing. With 0.205 ms median latency, NEXUS adds under 0.1% overhead to typical agent loops. Code, benchmarks, and the calibrated risk scorer are publicly released.
documents.notes: Abstract page shows submission 25 May 2026 although the arXiv ID is 2607.*; date recorded as shown on the page. Evaluated on a 128-instance synthetic benchmark plus R-Judge, AgentHarm and IPI. Session-state numbers cited in earlier search summaries are NOT in the abstract and are not recorded here. Metadata verified from the arXiv abstract page on 2026-11-13.
documents.title: NEXUS: Structured Runtime Safety for Tool-Using LLM Agents

documents.content:
## Claim
Zenity argues device-based AI (coding agents and personal AI tools on endpoints) is a distinct risk class. Its stated position is that EDR and DLP monitor processes and file activity but cannot observe what a coding agent decides, what it writes, where it sends data, or which external services and MCP servers it connects to.

## Threat vectors listed
Code and data exfiltration, destructive actions, prompt injection, lateral movement, and supply-chain risk via repositories, extensions and MCP servers.

## Caveat
Vendor marketing content; the visibility gap is asserted, not measured.
documents.notes: Source-type: vendor blog (Zenity).. Opening section read; remainder not reviewed.
documents.title: Device-Based AI Security: Protecting Endpoint AI Agents (Zenity)

documents.content:
## Claim (as attributed to Tenet Security)
Attacker-controlled instructions are POSTed into Sentry error events using only a public write-only DSN. AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) retrieved the events over MCP, did not distinguish them from real errors in Tenet's testing, and ran attacker-controlled commands with the developer's own privileges.

## Reported figures
Tenet reports an 85% exploitation success rate across tested agents and at least 2,388 organizations with injectable DSNs. In tested configurations the attack bypassed EDR, WAF, IAM and VPN because only authorized operations were performed with the developer's credentials.

## Caveat
These are Tenet's proof-of-concept results, not confirmed exploitation at scale (the CSA note says so). Sentry reportedly acknowledged the disclosure but declined root-cause remediation.
documents.notes: Source-type: industry research note (CSA Labs) summarizing vendor research by Tenet Security.. Key Takeaways and background read; full attack chain not reviewed.
documents.title: Agentjacking: MCP Injection Hijacks AI Coding Agents (Cloud Security Alliance research note)

documents.content:
## Points reported by a search excerpt (unverified)
- Claude Code reads project configuration automatically, so a malicious MCP server defined in those files can execute commands before the trust dialog appears.
- A Cursor issue where approval was tied to a plugin's name rather than a content hash of what was approved.

## To do
Read the article and confirm the CVE identifiers and affected versions before relying on this note.
documents.notes: Source-type: news article (Dark Reading).. NOT READ: the page returned HTTP 403 (bot wall) on 2026-11-13. The points below come from a web-search excerpt and should be verified against the article.

documents.content:
## Framing
Pillar says good coding-agent security does four things: find every agent on a developer machine, audit each one's configuration, block a dangerous action before it runs, and keep doing so if the developer or agent tries to disable the control.

## Claims
The guide compares thirteen tools on eight questions. It recommends Pillar, citing configuration parsing for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI and OpenCode, pre-action controls on three of them, and an MCP catalog of 23,000+ analyzed servers. It names Palo Alto Networks (Koi) and Noma as closest alternatives.

## Caveat
Self-recommending vendor comparison; treat the ranking and product claims as unverified.
documents.notes: Source-type: vendor blog (Pillar Security), a comparison that includes and recommends the publisher's own product.. Introduction read; the 13-tool comparison table was not reviewed.

documents.content:
## Claim
Workforce AI security focused on the browser for two years; coding agents, skills and MCP servers now run on laptops with real access to code, credentials and internal systems, and security teams lack visibility into what they do.

## Illustrative scenario
The post walks through a hypothetical: a sanctioned agent plus an approved Jira MCP server processes a ticket containing buried instructions to fetch and run an external script, exfiltrating a .env file. Every step looks legitimate in isolation.

## Caveat
The scenario is illustrative, not an incident report. Vendor content.

documents.content:
## Claim
Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor read local files, launch processes, use stored credentials and load MCP servers, skills, plugins and hooks. Backslash calls this the 'agentic fabric' and says EDR sees processes, MDM sees installed apps and proxies see traffic, but none connect a prompt, a component and a permission to the local action that followed.

## Evaluation criteria it proposes
Discover every agent and component on the device; map what each can reach; block unsafe local actions before they complete; preserve endpoint-level evidence for investigation.

## Cited statistic
Cites Latio's 2026 AI Security Market Report: 45% of surveyed practitioners named endpoint agents as their primary AI security concern, and teams with a dedicated AI security budget rose from 8% to 37% in a year (not independently checked).

## Caveat
Vendor-authored ranking.
documents.notes: Source-type: vendor blog (Backslash Security), a vendor ranking.. TL;DR and introduction read; the vendor-by-vendor sections were not reviewed.
documents.title: Top 7 Agentic Endpoint Security Companies CISOs Should Evaluate in 2026 (Backslash Security)

documents.content:
## Why Per-Turn Evaluation Is Not Enough: AI security: endpoint perspective, and tracking the trajectory of AI sessions, chats and transactions to detect crescendo and escalation attacks
Multi-turn attacks such as Crescendo (`arxiv-2404.01833`) start with benign-looking requests and escalate gradually by building on the model's own replies, so each individual turn can pass a stateless check while the conversation as a whole does not. Defenses in this collection therefore score the trajectory rather than the turn.

## Session-Level Detection Approaches
Collected literature — Great, Now Write an Article About That: The Crescendo Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreak Attack (arxiv-2404.01833); SoK: Evaluating Jailbreak Guardrails for Large Language Models (arxiv-2506.10597); ProbGuard: Proactive Runtime Monitoring for LLM Agent Safety via Probabilistic Prediction (arxiv-2508.00500); Defensive M2S: Training Guardrail Models on Compressed Multi-turn Conversations (arxiv-2601.00454); Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic Coding Assistants: A Systematic Analysis of Vulnerabilities in Skills, Tools, and Protocol Ecosystems (arxiv-2601.17548); Peak + Accumulation: A Proxy-Level Scoring Formula for Multi-Turn LLM Attack Detection (arxiv-2602.11247); DeepContext: Stateful Real-Time Detection of Multi-Turn Adversarial Intent Drift in LLMs (arxiv-2602.16935); A Systematic Survey of Security Threats and Defenses in LLM-Based AI Agents: A Layered Attack Surface Framework (arxiv-2604.23338); A Low-Latency Fraud Detection Layer for Detecting Adversarial Interaction Patterns in LLM-Powered Agents (arxiv-2605.01143); AgentTrust: Runtime Safety Evaluation and Interception for AI Agent Tool Use (arxiv-2605.04785); THRD: A Training-Free Multi-Turn Defense Framework for Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models (arxiv-2606.01738); PsychoPass: Geometric Profiling of Multi-Turn Adversarial LLM Conversations (arxiv-2606.03136); NEXUS: Structured Runtime Safety for Tool-Using LLM Agents (arxiv-2607.19356); Device-Based AI Security: Protecting Endpoint AI Agents (Zenity) (note-2026-zenity-device-based-ai-security); Agentjacking: MCP Injection Hijacks AI Coding Agents (Cloud Security Alliance research note) (note-2026-csa-agentjacking-mcp-sentry); How AI Coding Tools Crushed the Endpoint Security Fortress (Dark Reading) (note-2026-darkreading-ai-coding-tools-endpoint); Best AI Coding Agent Security Tools for the Enterprise (2026) (Pillar Security) (note-2026-pillar-ai-coding-agent-security-tools); Securing AI on Endpoints: How to Govern AI Tools, Coding Agents, and MCP Connections (Lasso Security) (note-2026-lasso-securing-ai-on-endpoints); Top 7 Agentic Endpoint Security Companies CISOs Should Evaluate in 2026 (Backslash Security) (note-2026-backslash-agentic-endpoint-security-top7) — spans: (1) **conversation-level scoring** (Peak + Accumulation's proxy-layer formula, THRD's time-evolving risk score, DeepContext's recurrent hidden state, PsychoPass's embedding-space geometry, Defensive M2S's compressed histories); (2) **agent runtime monitoring** over tool calls and execution traces (NEXUS, AgentTrust, ProbGuard, and a fraud-detection-style feature layer for adversarial interaction patterns); and (3) **taxonomies and surveys** (SoK on jailbreak guardrails, SoK on prompt injection against agentic coding assistants, and a layered attack-surface survey with a temporality axis that reports no benchmark coverage of cross-session failures).

## Endpoint View & Open Gaps
On the endpoint, vendor and CSA material argues that EDR sees a trusted agent process doing authorized work and so cannot see agent-level manipulation (for example MCP-delivered injection). Much of the evidence is small, synthetic, or vendor-authored, results are not comparable across papers, and cross-session attacks remain largely unaddressed.

identifiers.research_topic: AI security: endpoint perspective, and tracking the trajectory of AI sessions, chats and transactions to detect crescendo and escalation attacks

documents.notes: Automated multi-paper synthesis and taxonomy bridge for topic: 'AI security: endpoint perspective, and tracking the trajectory of AI sessions, chats and transactions to detect crescendo and escalation attacks'.
documents.title: Research Synthesis: AI security: endpoint perspective, and tracking the trajectory of AI sessions, chats and transactions to detect crescendo and escalation attacks

documents.content:
## Question
How do we detect AI misuse that no single prompt reveals — Crescendo-style slow escalation across a chat, session, or sequence of transactions — and what changes when the AI application is an agent running on an endpoint?

## Bottom line
- Per-turn checks are structurally blind to gradual escalation. Every defense in this collection adds state: a score, a hidden state, a geometry, or a risk chain that persists across turns.
- The evidence is early. Most results use small, synthetic, or template-generated data and no shared benchmark exists, so headline numbers (F1 0.84, recall 90.8%, ASR 0.2-4.0%) are not comparable across papers.
- The endpoint is a separate problem. EDR sees a trusted agent process doing authorized work; the manipulation happens in what the agent reads and decides. Endpoint vendors and CSA argue this; the numbers behind it are vendor-authored.
- Cross-session accumulation is the least-covered case. One survey reports no benchmark coverage for it.

## The attack: Crescendo (arXiv 2404.01833)
Starts with a benign question on the topic, then escalates by referencing the model's own replies. Each turn looks acceptable alone. Reported high attack success across ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama-2/3 70B and Anthropic chat models; the automated variant Crescendomation beat other jailbreaks on an AdvBench subset (29-61% on GPT-4, 49-71% on Gemini-Pro, per the abstract).

## Conversation-level detection: what each approach adds
| Paper | Core idea | Reported result (author-reported) |
|---|---|---|
| Peak + Accumulation (2602.11247) | Proxy-layer score from peak turn risk, persistence ratio, category diversity; no LLM call. Shows a weighted average converges to the per-turn score, so a 20-turn attack scores like one suspicious turn. | 90.8% recall at 1.20% FPR, F1 85.9% on 10,654 conversations (588 attacks, WildJailbreak vs WildChat) |
| DeepContext (2602.16935) | RNN over turn embeddings carries a hidden state, capturing accumulated risk | F1 0.84 vs 0.67 (Llama-Prompt-Guard-2, Granite-Guardian); sub-20 ms on a T4 |
| THRD (2606.01738) | Training-free: turn risk + cross-turn intent escalation + response facilitation, combined with attenuation and trend-aware scoring | ASR 0.2-4.0%; over 70% of multi-turn attacks need Turn 2 or later to detect |
| PsychoPass (2606.03136) | Conversation as a path in embedding space; geometric features predict attack before harmful output | Early signal from short prefixes; near-perfect naive scores are largely a turn-count confound |
| Defensive M2S (2601.00454) | Compress multi-turn history to single-turn for guardrail training/inference | 93.8% recall, 94.6% fewer inference tokens (SafeDialBench) |

## Agent and transaction-level monitoring
- Fraud-detection-style layer (2605.01143): models risk over interaction trajectories from session dynamics, tool usage and execution context; XGBoost on 42 features, reported 9x faster than LLM-based detectors, on a synthetic 12,000-interaction corpus.
- AgentTrust (2605.04785): intercepts tool calls pre-execution with a verdict (allow/warn/block/review); includes RiskChain detection for multi-step chains and shell deobfuscation.
- NEXUS (2607.19356): structured-plan monitor with deterministic rules, argument inspection and a calibrated risk score choosing allow/block/confirm/revise; 0.205 ms median latency.
- ProbGuard (2508.00500): learns a Markov chain over abstracted execution states and intervenes when the probability of staying safe drops. Evaluated on autonomous driving and embodied household agents, not on chat security, but it is the clearest "predict the trajectory" formulation.

## Endpoint view
- Prompt injection against coding assistants is a first-class vulnerability class; a 78-study meta-analysis reports attack success above 85% against defenses under adaptive attacks and most of 18 defenses under 50% mitigation (2601.17548; consolidation of prior work).
- Agentjacking (CSA note summarizing Tenet Security PoC): instructions injected via Sentry events were retrieved over MCP and executed with developer privileges; reported 85% success across tested agents and EDR bypass in tested configurations. These are the discoverer's proof-of-concept figures, not observed exploitation.
- Vendor framing (Zenity, Lasso, Backslash, Pillar): the endpoint needs discovery of agents and MCP servers, pre-action blocking, and evidence that links a prompt, a component and a permission to the local action that followed. Backslash states EDR, MDM and proxies each see one slice and none connect them.

## My synthesis (inference, not from the sources)
1. Keep both a per-turn score and persistent state. Peak catches the spike; accumulation and persistence catch the slow rise; a decay term (THRD) prevents old benign context from masking a late push.
2. Key state on identity (user, device, account), not session ID, or the cross-session case is invisible by construction.
3. Include the assistant's output as a signal (THRD's response evaluator), since Crescendo steers using the model's own replies.
4. Control for turn count when evaluating. PsychoPass shows length alone can look like detection.
5. On endpoints, log the chain not the event: input source, tool/MCP component, permission used, resulting process/file/network action, under one correlation ID, so trajectory analysis and EDR telemetry can be joined.
6. Treat transaction sequences like fraud: velocity, diversity of categories touched, and risk-chain patterns, with a cheap model in the hot path and an LLM judge for ambiguous cases.

## Corrections to my first-pass summary
Reading the abstracts showed several details I had passed along from search summaries are not supported by them, so they are not recorded in this database:
- NEXUS: a "0/95 to 95/95 with session memory" result is not in the abstract (it reports a 128-instance synthetic benchmark, F1 0.949). Unverified; may be in the paper body.
- Fraud-detection paper: "cross-turn signals contribute most" is not in the abstract (it mentions ablation studies only).
- AgentTrust: the abstract does not say "seven" risk chains.
- Layered attack-surface survey: the two-phase plant-then-trigger framing is not in the abstract; the supported claim is that benchmarks give no coverage of cross-session failure modes.
- Dark Reading article: unreadable (HTTP 403); the note is flagged unverified.

## Open questions
- Which of these hold up on organic traces rather than synthetic or authored ones?
- What is the false-positive cost on long, legitimately escalating work (security research, red-team tooling, incident response)?
- How do session-scoped monitors handle memory/persistence features that carry state between sessions?
- Can endpoint telemetry and conversation scoring be joined without capturing sensitive prompt content?

## Next reading
Full text of NEXUS, the fraud-detection framework and the layered attack-surface survey (to check the claims above); the Dark Reading article; Tenet Security's original agentjacking write-up.
